item.title: Are wildfires making the future uninsurable?
item.description:
Over the past decade, increasingly catastrophic wildfires have wrought unprecedented destruction and upended the basic math of the insurance industry. In some of the riskiest parts of the country, homeowners have seen spiking premiums or lost their coverage altogether.

Today on the show, we travel to the forested foothills of Northern California to see how communities in wildfire-prone areas are trying to conjure the private insurance market back into existence. What actually happens when a megafire comes knocking at your door. And what all this means for the biggest question: In the age of climate change, could the future simply become uninsurable?

For more about how natural disasters are changing the insurance industry: 

  • Insurance in the time of climate change
  • Inside the insurance industry’s destruction lab
  • Episode 797: Flood Money 
  • Episode 570: The Fine Print

item.title: How bodegas led to the Yemeni coffeehouse explosion
item.description:
There is a long-standing tradition of different immigrant groups arriving in the U.S. and specializing in one particular type of business. Think, nail salons run by people from Vietnam or Gujarati Indians owning motels and hotels.

Yemenis are another immigrant community that has largely clustered around one industry, in their case, bodegas and small grocery stores. There are thousands of these shops all over the country, despite Yemeni-Americans only making up around one-fortieth of one percent of the U.S. population, according to the last census. 

In the past 9 years, a new business success story has been built on top of that foundation: Yemeni coffee houses.

Today on the show, why some immigrant groups concentrate in a single industry, while others spread out to work in all sorts of jobs. And what it’s like for the next generation to try to expand on their parents’ success.
